resources.string: Hardcoded credential in “%1$s” — anyone who decompiles the APK can read it. Move it to a build config, an environment variable or the Android Keystore.
This looks like a real API key committed into the source. Revoke it, then load it from configuration instead of a literal.
User name and password embedded in a URL. They end up in logs, crash reports and proxy history — pass them as separate credentials.
SQL built by string concatenation — SQL injection. Use a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders, or rawQuery with a selectionArgs array.
SQL built with String.format — the arguments are not escaped. Use a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders instead.
A concatenated statement is executed directly. Bind the values as parameters rather than pasting them into the SQL text.
%1$s is broken and must not be used for passwords or signatures. Use SHA-256 for integrity, and bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 for passwords.
Weak cipher “%1$s”. Use AES with GCM; ECB mode leaks the structure of the plaintext.
This accepts every TLS certificate, which removes the protection TLS exists to provide and makes the connection trivially interceptable.
Plain http:// to a public host — the traffic is readable and modifiable on the way. Use https://.
Random and Math.random are predictable and must not generate tokens, keys or salts. Use SecureRandom.
World-readable/writable mode makes this file available to every app on the device. It has been deprecated since API 17 and throws since API 24.
addJavascriptInterface exposes Java methods to page JavaScript. On loaded remote content this is remote code execution.
JavaScript is enabled in a WebView that loads a URL. Make sure the content is yours and cannot be replaced in transit.
Secrets written to external storage are readable by other apps and survive uninstall. Keep them in app-private storage or the Keystore.
